header.question:
A document in the library contains this sentence:

> Attackers may also use indirect prompt injection attacks to hijack a GenAI AGENT, causing it to perform a malicious, attacker-specified task instead of (or in addition to) its intended, user-provided task [353].

Check what the sentence says about the work it cites against that work in the library. Does the cited source support it? Cite the page(s) of the cited source that show what it actually says.

args.text:
Verdict: supported

The sentence is on page 52 of NIST AI 100-2e2025 (PDF p. 65), in the "Integrity Attacks" part of the indirect prompt injection section: "Attackers may also use indirect prompt injection attacks to hijack a GenAI AGENT, causing it to perform a malicious, attacker-specified task instead of (or in addition to) its intended, user-provided task [353]." (nist:ai-100-2/r3/p65)

Reference [353] is "U.S. AI Safety Institute Technical Staff. Strengthening ai agent hijacking evaluations, 2024" (nist:ai-100-2/r3/p109). That is the NIST CAISI technical blog *Strengthening AI Agent Hijacking Evaluations*, which is in the library as nist:technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations/r1.

The blog supports the core of the claim:

- It defines the term: "agent hijacking, a type of indirect prompt injection in which an attacker inserts malicious instructions into data that may be ingested by an AI agent, causing it to take unintended, harmful actions." (nist:technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations/r1/b3)
- It says the attacker's data is meant "to 'hijack' the agent to complete a different and potentially harmful task." (nist:technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations/r1/b10)
- It describes the evaluation unit as a scenario in which "an agent is asked to complete a legitimate user task but encounters data containing an attack that tries to direct the agent to complete a malicious injection task." (nist:technical-blog-strengthening-ai-agent-hijacking-evaluations/r1/b13)

The "instead of (or in addition to)" wording is the survey's own gloss. The blog frames hijacking as the agent completing a different task, and does not say "in addition to". So the claim is supported in substance, but the "in addition to" part is not in the cited source.

Note that the cited source is a short blog post about AgentDojo experiments, not a taxonomy. It does not discuss the other attack types the sentence leads into.
